These checked-in deterministic ZIP fixtures use a fixed 2020-01-01 timestamp.
Entries use DEFLATE, except
`mimetype`, which is stored uncompressed as required for MIME recognition.

They contain small synthetic payloads, not complete Office documents, ebooks,
Java programs, or Android apps. They exercise real ZIP container structure and
package naming/MIME conventions without including third-party document content.
The DOCX fixture also has a comment longer than two scanner read chunks, with a
misleading EOCD signature near its end. All fixtures are project test data under
the repository's MIT license.

The `real.*`, `real89.gif`, `real-progressive.jpg`, `real-dib.ico`,
`real256.ico`, and animated image fixtures are small images generated with
Pillow from a project-owned RGB gradient. They contain valid encoded pixels,
not placeholder image bodies. ICO fixtures cover multiple PNG/DIB frames and
the zero-byte directory dimension that means 256 pixels. Test code mutates
copies in memory to exercise corruption and false-positive rejection.

`real.sqlite` and `large-page.sqlite` are checked-in databases using page sizes
of 512 and 65536 bytes. Each
contains a small table with a text value and the project-owned PNG as a BLOB.
Both pass SQLite's `PRAGMA integrity_check`; the latter exercises the special
page-size header value of 1. The embedded image also tests duplicate suppression.

`real.ogg` (Vorbis), `real.opus` (Opus), and `real.ogv` (Theora) were generated
with FFmpeg from a 440 Hz sine wave or solid blue 32×32 frames, with bitexact
flags and stripped metadata. They contain actual encoded media; FFmpeg decodes
all three without errors. Test-created Ogg pages independently calculate their
CRC bit by bit to exercise invalid sequence numbers and packet continuations.

`embedded-image.zip` stores the project PNG without compression, with a fixed
2020 timestamp. It verifies that a complete archive produces one candidate,
while a damaged archive still exposes its independently recoverable image.

The `formats/` fixtures are generated by `cargo xtask fixtures` using Rust encoders and explicit on-disk records. They are project-owned, inert parser fixtures under MIT. MSI/MSP/MST contain minimal CFB root metadata, and RPM/DEX contain minimal framing; these are not working installers or applications. PE certificate records are structural examples, not valid signatures. See `docs/FILE_FORMAT_RESEARCH.md` for primary sources and coverage limits.

`deleted-journal-ext4.img.gz` and `deleted-journal-ext3.img.gz` are 3 MiB
volumes made with `mkfs.ext4`/`mkfs.ext3 -b 1024`, mounted through udisks and
written by the Linux 7.0 kernel driver: the disk was filled with alternating
16 KiB files, every other one was deleted, then a 96 KB generated document
(`Docs/Holiday plan.pdf`, rebuilt by `tests/ext_journal.rs`) was saved into
the gaps and deleted. The driver erased its block list and name; only the
journal still holds them.

`deleted-blockmap-ext2.img.gz` is a 3 MiB volume made with `mkfs.ext2 -b 1024`
and written by the Linux 7.0 kernel driver the same way, with a 322 KB
generated document (rebuilt by `tests/ext_block_maps.rs`) saved into the gaps
and deleted. Its inode is cleared; only the freed indirect and double-indirect
blocks still list where its pieces are.

Mounting records the mount point, including the local user name, in each
superblock's "last mounted" field and in superblock copies in the journal. That
field is zeroed in all three images (`debugfs -w -R 'ssv last_mounted ""'`
after zeroing the 64 bytes, which also refreshes the ext4 superblock checksum),
and they are packed with `gzip -9 -n` so the archive holds no file name or
time. The ext4 journal's copy of that block keeps its original journal
checksum; the volume is clean, so the journal is never replayed.
